questions.question: What is a struct in Go, and how do you define one?
questions.title: Defining structs in Go
questions.direct_answer: A struct is a value type that groups a fixed set of named fields into one record. Define a named struct with `type Name struct { ... }`, then create values of that type to represent related data such as a user, order, or coordinate. A struct holds data; methods are declared separately with a receiver, and every field receives its zero value when no value is supplied.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether a struct is understood as a typed value with fields rather than as a class declaration.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming methods are written inside the struct or that an uninitialized struct has no usable value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the value-copy rule and the separate receiver-based method declaration.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A struct groups named fields into one value type.
Fields may have different types and are selected with `value.Field`.
Unspecified fields receive their type's zero value.
Methods are declared outside the struct body with a receiver.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A struct is Go's way to combine related data into one value with a known shape. A declaration such as `type User struct { Name string; Active bool }` creates a new named type with two fields. Each `User` value contains both fields, and code accesses them with selectors such as `user.Name`.

Structs are value types. Assigning one struct to another or passing it by value copies the struct value. The fields inside still follow their own rules, so copying a struct that contains a slice copies the slice descriptor, not the slice's backing array. That distinction matters when a record contains reference-like fields.

For example, `var user User` is already usable: `Name` is the empty string and `Active` is false. A composite literal such as `User{Name: "Asha", Active: true}` supplies selected values. Methods do not appear inside the declaration; `func (u User) Label() string` is written separately and associates behaviour with the named type.

A struct is a good fit when the program knows the fields and their meanings at compile time. It is less suitable for truly dynamic keys, where a map may be clearer. The main idea is that a struct gives related data a named, compiler-checked shape while remaining an ordinary Go value.

sections.title: A record with a compile-time shape
sections.content:
A struct declaration describes a layout, not an object hierarchy. Every field has a name and a type, so the compiler can reject misspelled fields and invalid assignments. The declaration may contain fields or embedded fields, but it does not contain method bodies.

A named struct can receive methods because it is a defined type. The data and behaviour are connected through the receiver in each method declaration. This keeps the record shape visible while allowing different APIs to work with the value, a pointer to it, or an interface that its methods satisfy.

sections.title: How data and behaviour meet
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[type User struct] --> B[Name string]
  A --> C[Active bool]
  D[User value] --> B
  D --> C
  E[Method with User receiver] --> D
```

questions.question: What is the zero value of a Go struct?
questions.title: The zero value of a struct
questions.direct_answer: The zero value of a struct is a struct value whose fields each hold the zero value of their own type. Numeric fields are zero, booleans are false, strings are empty, and pointer, slice, map, function, channel, and interface fields are nil. A well-designed type often makes this state safe and useful, but fields such as nil maps still have their normal operation limits.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of recursive field zeroing and the difference between a valid zero struct and valid operations on every nil field.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling the zero value unusable, or assuming a nil map can be written because a nil slice can be appended to.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate the language rule from the API choice to make a type zero-value-friendly.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A zero struct exists without calling a constructor.
Every field independently receives its type's zero value.
Reading a nil map is safe, but writing to it panics.
Constructors are still useful when invariants or resources must be established.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A variable declared as `var x T` always has a value in Go. When `T` is a struct, that value is built by assigning the zero value to every field. A nested struct is zeroed recursively, while fields such as pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, and interfaces begin as nil. There is no uninitialized-memory state visible to ordinary Go code.

This makes many simple types pleasant to use. For example, a `Counter` with an integer field can start counting immediately because zero is a sensible initial count. Types in the standard library such as `bytes.Buffer` and `sync.Mutex` are deliberately useful at their zero values, so callers do not need constructors just to establish valid state.

Zero-valued does not mean every operation is valid. A nil map field can be read, but assigning a key to it panics until code allocates the map. A nil pointer field cannot be dereferenced. The containing struct itself is valid; its methods must respect the state of those fields.

A constructor remains appropriate when a type needs mandatory data, validation, an allocated collection, or an external resource. The useful design test is whether accidental `var T` usage is safe. If the zero value cannot represent a valid state, the package should expose a constructor and make the invariant clear.

sections.title: Zeroing happens field by field
sections.content:
The language does not run a hidden constructor. It applies the ordinary zero-value rule to the struct's fields. For a nested struct, the same rule continues through its fields. This creates a deterministic baseline that can be inspected, compared when the type is comparable, and passed to methods.

Whether that baseline is useful is an API-design decision. A numeric accumulator naturally starts at zero. A client that requires a URL and authenticated transport probably needs construction. Safe methods can lazily initialize an internal map, but that policy should be deliberate rather than assumed.

sections.title: Fields inside a zero-valued struct
sections.content:
| Field type | Zero value | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|
| `int` | `0` | Ready for arithmetic |
| `string` | `""` | Valid empty text |
| `bool` | `false` | May represent the default state |
| `[]T` | `nil` | Range and append work |
| `map[K]V` | `nil` | Reads work; writes panic |
| `*T` | `nil` | Must be checked before dereference |

questions.question: When can Go struct values be compared with `==`?
questions.title: Struct comparability in Go
questions.direct_answer: A struct type is comparable when every one of its fields is comparable. Two values of that type are equal when all corresponding non-blank fields are equal. Strings, booleans, numbers, pointers, channels, interfaces, arrays of comparable elements, and comparable structs may participate; a slice, map, or function field makes the entire struct non-comparable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether struct equality is derived from field types and separated from domain-specific equality.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to compare a struct that contains a slice, or assuming direct equality compares slice contents.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the dynamic-value boundary when a comparable interface field contains a non-comparable value.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Every field must be comparable for the struct to be comparable.
Equality checks corresponding fields using their normal equality rules.
Slice, map, and function fields make a struct non-comparable.
Comparable structs may be used as map keys.
An interface comparison can still panic if its dynamic value is non-comparable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go permits `==` and `!=` on a struct only when all of that struct's fields are comparable. Equality then compares corresponding fields. A `Point` containing two integers is comparable, and a `UserKey` containing strings and an integer is comparable, so either type can also be used as a map key.

Comparability is structural. Adding a slice, map, or function field changes the property of the whole struct because those types cannot be compared with `==` except against nil where allowed. For example, `type Report struct { Name string; Tags []string }` cannot be compared directly, even when both `Tags` slices happen to contain the same elements. Code must define the intended equality, such as comparing fields and using `slices.Equal` for the slice.

Blank fields are ignored when struct values are compared, but this is uncommon in application records. Interface fields require extra care: the interface type is comparable, yet comparing two interface values panics if their identical dynamic type is itself non-comparable, such as a slice.

I use direct struct equality for small value objects whose fields have clear value semantics. For records containing collections, functions, or resources, I write an explicit equality function that documents what identity means. That remains correct when representation and business equality are not the same thing.

sections.title: Comparability flows inward from every field
sections.content:
The compiler decides struct comparability from the declared field types, not from the values present in one instance. A nil slice still has slice type, so placing it in a struct does not make that instance comparable. Arrays differ from slices: an array is comparable when its element type is comparable.

Direct equality is exact field equality. It does not perform fuzzy floating-point comparison, normalize text, or compare collection contents. Domain rules may therefore need a named `Equal` function even when `==` is legal.

sections.title: Decide whether a struct is comparable
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Inspect every field type] --> B{Any slice, map, or function?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Struct is not comparable]
  B -- No --> D{Every nested array or struct comparable?}
  D -- No --> C
  D -- Yes --> E[Struct supports == and map keys]
```
